title: Objects
description: Model real-world entities using key-value properties, access known and dynamic keys using dot and bracket notation, and query arrays of objects.

objectives.statement: Construct objects with key-value properties to model structured entities.
Access and mutate object properties using dot notation for static keys and bracket notation for dynamic expressions.
Traverse and manipulate composite collections structured as arrays of objects.

content.title: Modeling Real-World Entities with Objects
content.hook: Arrays store ordered lists of items, but how do you describe a single item that has a name, an email, and an active status?
content.context: JavaScript objects group related pieces of state into key-value pairs called properties. Objects allow you to pass around a single, coherent representation of a learner, a course, or a shopping cart item instead of juggling multiple disconnected variables.
goals: Construct objects using object literal syntax.
Access static properties with dot notation and dynamic keys with bracket notation.
Manipulate composite arrays of objects representing application collections.

content.title: Property Access: Dot Notation vs Bracket Notation
content.description: Visual diagram comparing static dot notation (user.role looks up the literal property named 'role') versus dynamic bracket notation (user[fieldKey] evaluates variable fieldKey first to determine which property to inspect).

feedback.correct: Spot on! user[key] evaluates the variable 'role' to get 'Engineer', while user.key looks up the literal property 'key' to get 'SecretKey123'.
feedback.incorrect: Remember: brackets evaluate variables (user[key] -> user['role']), while dots look up literal names (user.key).

hints.content: user[key] evaluates the variable key ('role') and accesses user['role'], which is 'Engineer'.
user.key literally accesses the property named 'key', which is 'SecretKey123'.

content.question: What happens when you read a property that does not exist on a valid object, such as `const user = { name: 'Alex' }; console.log(user.age);`?

options.text: JavaScript returns `undefined` without throwing an error.
JavaScript throws a ReferenceError and crashes.
JavaScript automatically creates the property and assigns it `0`.

feedback.correct: Great eye! learner.name, learner['xp'], and learner['current-level'] are all valid. learner.current-level causes a syntax error.
feedback.incorrect: learner.current-level is invalid because JavaScript treats the hyphen as a minus operator. Bracket notation is required for keys with hyphens.

hints.content: Keys with hyphens cannot be accessed with dot notation because the hyphen is parsed as subtraction.

content.question: Given `const learner = { name: 'Jordan', xp: 450, 'current-level': 3 };`, which of the following expressions successfully retrieve values without syntax errors?

testCases.assertion: typeof createLearner === 'function' && (() => { const l = createLearner('Sam', 'sam@forge.dev'); return l && l.name === 'Sam' && l.email === 'sam@forge.dev' && l.xp === 0; })()

testCases.description: getDynamicField retrieves property using bracket lookup
testCases.assertion: typeof getDynamicField === 'function' && (() => { const item = { status: 'completed', score: 98 }; return getDynamicField(item, 'status') === 'completed' && getDynamicField(item, 'score') === 98; })()
typeof addXp === 'function' && (() => { const user = { name: 'Morgan', xp: 100 }; const res = addXp(user, 50); return res.xp === 150 && user.xp === 150; })()

feedback.correct: Fantastic! You constructed object entities, performed dynamic bracket lookups, and updated property state.
feedback.incorrect: Verify your implementations: createLearner sets initial xp to 0, getDynamicField uses brackets entity[fieldName], and addXp increments learner.xp.

hints.content: In createLearner, return { name, email, xp: 0 };
In addXp, write learner.xp += points; return learner;

content.title: Build Learner Entity Helpers
content.prompt:
Implement three object helper functions:
1. createLearner(name, email): Returns a new object with name, email, and xp initialized to 0.
2. getDynamicField(entity, fieldName): Returns entity[fieldName] using dynamic bracket notation.
3. addXp(learner, points): Increments learner.xp by points and returns the updated learner object.

feedback.correct: Well analyzed! Arrays structure the collection sequence, while objects encapsulate the multi-attribute records.
feedback.incorrect: Please write at least 30 characters discussing how arrays of objects structure lists of entities in UI development.

content.prompt: Why are arrays of objects the most common data structure in modern frontend development when working with APIs and databases?

content.title: Objects Takeaway
takeaways: Objects group related attributes into key-value pairs representing domain entities.
Dot notation (obj.key) is ideal for known keys; bracket notation (obj[key]) is required for dynamic variable keys and special characters.
Arrays of objects combine lists and entity structures into the primary data format of web applications.
